designNotes: Causes are EXPLANATORY HYPOTHESES — not signals, not pathways. A cause is the answer to the question 'why is this person losing hair', stated at a granularity a clinician would dictate. Signals are observations. Pathways are mechanisms. Causes are competing explanations that consume the active pathway graph (and a small set of direct signal cues) and emit a ranked posterior distribution. Ranking is Bayesian: each cause carries a clinical prior, every cause→pathway link is a log-likelihood-ratio (LLR) weighted by pathway activation, every cause→signal link is an LLR weighted by signal confidence, and conflicting/inhibitory evidence subtracts from the log-score. Final posterior is the softmax over log-scores. Dissent is the second-best cause's posterior; high dissent prevents a single-cause framing and routes toward 'multifactorial-hair-loss' as the leading explanation. Confidence is propagated from underlying pathway confidence and signal evidence-tier — a cause cannot be more confident than the evidence base it stands on.

causes.name: Androgen-Driven Miniaturization
causes.description: DHT-mediated follicle downsizing produces the dominant fraction of progressive thinning. The explanation answers 'why are the hairs becoming finer'. It does not say 'AGA grade' — that is a severity property — it says 'androgen signalling is the prime mover'.
causes.priorRationale: AGA is the most prevalent hair-loss etiology across adult populations of both sexes (~30% lifetime prevalence over the assessment age band). Prior is the base rate before any evidence is inspected.

contributingPathways.notes: This is the definitional pathway. Without measurable miniaturization activation the cause cannot lead.
Female-pattern AGA frequently co-activates endocrine pathway (PCOS, peri/postmeno).
Heavy active shedding without thinning weakens the miniaturization hypothesis.
Patchy autoimmune loss is a structurally different etiology.

dissentRules.notes: If hormonal-hair-loss posterior exceeds this cause by more than 0.05, leadership flips. Co-leading (within 0.05) is permitted and surfaced as 'co-explanation'.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Androgen-mediated terminal-to-vellus conversion is the dominant explanation for the observed thinning topology.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Your hair is getting finer because of how your body is responding to hormones over time — a hereditary pattern.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: DHT-driven dermal-papilla signaling shortens anagen and reduces follicle volume across successive cycles.

legacyMappings.notes: Severity-driven hard floor; not a separate cause.

causes.name: Stress-Driven Telogen Effluvium
causes.description: Premature anagen→telogen transition triggered by physical or psychological stressors. Explains diffuse shedding 2–4 months after the precipitant. Distinct from miniaturization: follicle architecture is intact.
causes.priorRationale: Telogen effluvium is the second-most prevalent presentation in adult clinics; postpartum, post-illness, and chronic-stress phenotypes dominate.

contributingPathways.notes: Coexistence is possible but dominant miniaturization shifts leadership to androgenic cause.

dissentRules.notes: Postpartum cases often co-lead with hormonal-hair-loss; permit co-explanation under 0.05 spread.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Diffuse synchronized telogen release triggered by an identifiable precipitant; architectural follicle integrity preserved.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: A stress event 2–4 months ago pushed many hairs into a resting phase, which now show up as visible shedding.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Stress-axis activation accelerates anagen-to-telogen transition; shedding lags the precipitant by one telogen cycle.

legacyMappings.notes: Pregnancy locks treatments; cause modeling treats as TE precipitant.

causes.name: Nutritional Hair Stress
causes.description: Hair phenotype attributable to micronutrient or substrate insufficiency — iron, vitamin D, protein, B-complex — manifesting as diffuse thinning, brittle hair, or telogen-spectrum shedding. Distinct from gut-axis cause (absorption-side) and from generic TE (substrate is the named driver).
causes.priorRationale: Documented deficiency or strong dietary risk pattern is present in ~10–12% of the assessment population at first encounter.

contributingPathways.notes: Nutritional deficits commonly precipitate TE; the cause is named for the driver, not the mechanism.

dissentRules.notes: Frequently co-leads with TE; permit co-explanation.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Substrate insufficiency for follicular proliferation — iron, D, B-complex, or protein — is the dominant explanation.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Your hair is reflecting a nutrient gap; restoring substrate restores cycling.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Reduced ferritin and 25-OH-vitamin-D constrain matrix proliferation; correction reverses the phenotype within a telogen cycle.

causes.name: Hormonal Hair Loss
causes.description: Hair loss whose dominant driver is an endocrine perturbation — thyroid (hypo/hyper), PCOS, peri/menopause, postpartum hormonal shift. The named driver is the endocrine state, even when downstream mechanism is telogen or miniaturization.
causes.priorRationale: Endocrine-attributable hair loss is present in ~14% of the female assessment population; lower among males where it routes to androgenic.

contributingPathways.notes: Endocrine-driven miniaturization (e.g. PCOS-AGA) is captured here rather than under androgenic cause when endocrine signals dominate.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Identifiable endocrine perturbation (thyroid, PCOS, peri/menopause) is the named driver of the observed loss.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: A hormonal shift is the leading explanation; correcting the underlying endocrine state typically improves the hair phenotype.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Thyroid, androgen, and estrogen axes modulate follicle cycling; perturbation produces phenotype-specific loss patterns.

causes.name: Metabolic Hair Dysfunction
causes.description: Hair loss driven primarily by insulin-glucose dysregulation, adiposity, or PCOS-with-metabolic phenotype. Frequently co-leads with hormonal cause; named separately when metabolic markers dominate the evidence base.
causes.priorRationale: Standalone metabolic-driven hair loss is uncommon as a sole explanation; usually appears as a co-explanation with hormonal or androgenic.

dissentRules.notes: Rarely the sole leader; expected to co-explain in most positive cases.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Insulin–androgen axis cross-talk is the named driver of the follicular phenotype.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Metabolic factors — sugar regulation, weight, related hormonal patterns — are the primary explanation here.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Hyperinsulinaemia raises bioavailable androgens via SHBG suppression, amplifying miniaturization risk.

causes.name: Autoimmune Hair Loss
causes.description: T-cell-mediated targeting of the follicle — alopecia areata spectrum and scarring forms. Distinguished by patchy or well-demarcated loss, history of areata, scarring, and immune co-morbidities.
causes.priorRationale: Low base rate (~2–5%) but very high signal specificity when its primary markers fire.

dissentRules.notes: When primary markers (patchy/AA-history/scarring) fire, this cause should lead with low dissent.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Immune-mediated follicular targeting is the named driver, supported by patchy topology and/or areata/scarring history.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Your immune system is reacting against the follicles; treatment focuses on calming that response.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Loss of immune privilege at the follicle bulge with CD8+ T-cell infiltration produces the areata phenotype; scarring forms reflect irreversible perifollicular fibrosis.

causes.name: Gut–Hair Axis Dysfunction
causes.description: Hair loss whose dominant explanation is absorption-side gut dysfunction — IBS, chronic constipation, GERD, microbiome-driven inflammation — producing functional substrate insufficiency and systemic low-grade inflammation.
causes.priorRationale: Reported gut-driven phenotype prevalence in the assessment population. Frequently co-leads with nutritional-hair-stress.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Functional malabsorption and gut inflammation are the named upstream drivers of the substrate insufficiency manifesting in hair.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Your gut and hair are connected — chronic gut symptoms are reducing how much your follicles can build with.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Chronic mucosal inflammation reduces iron and B-complex bioavailability while systemic cytokine load suppresses anagen.

causes.name: Inflammatory Scalp Dysfunction
causes.description: Scalp-surface and perifollicular inflammation as the named driver — seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff-with-itching, pustular folliculitis, psoriatic scalp. Amplifies miniaturization downstream but stands as its own cause when inflammation signals dominate.
causes.priorRationale: Inflammatory scalp dermatoses are common but typically modify rather than lead. Leads when miniaturization signals are absent or weak.

contributingPathways.notes: When miniaturization is dominant, scalp inflammation is downgraded to amplifier rather than primary cause.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Perifollicular and surface inflammation is the named driver; resolving the scalp-surface dermatosis restores cycling.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: The scalp environment around the follicle is inflamed; calming it is the primary lever here.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Malassezia-driven seborrhoeic inflammation and cytokine load disrupt anagen maintenance and pigmentation.

causes.name: Hair Shaft Damage Syndrome
causes.description: Loss explained by shaft-level mechanical, chemical, thermal, or environmental damage — not follicular dysfunction. Hair appears to be 'falling out' but the loss is breakage at the shaft, with intact follicles.
causes.priorRationale: Mid-shaft breakage as the sole explanation is relatively uncommon; commonly co-presents with other causes.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: Cuticle/cortex compromise from extrinsic exposures is the named driver; follicular architecture is intact.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Your hair is breaking, not falling — the strands are damaged by heat, chemicals, or environment, not the roots.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Repeated thermal and oxidative insults degrade cuticular integrity, producing mid-shaft fracture under normal mechanical load.

causes.name: Multifactorial Hair Loss
causes.description: Composite explanation reserved for cases where three or more pathways are simultaneously above the activation threshold AND no single cause dominates by more than the dissent ceiling. NOT a default — it is a structural verdict that the case cannot be honestly explained by one driver. Surfaces the top contributing causes as co-leads.
causes.priorRationale: Deliberately low prior. Multifactorial is not a fallback; it must EARN its leadership through the multi-pathway compositeness rule.

compositeRule.notes: If ≥3 pathways exceed 0.40 activation AND the gap between the top two single-cause posteriors is <0.06, multifactorial-hair-loss promotes to lead. Otherwise it remains a candidate but not the lead.

dissentRules.notes: Multifactorial leadership is granted ONLY via compositeRule. Outside that gate it remains a candidate. High dissent is expected — that is the point of this cause.

explainabilityMetadata.doctorFraming: No single driver dominates; the case requires a composite explanation across at least three pathways. Treatment must address the top co-leading causes in parallel.
explainabilityMetadata.patientFraming: Several causes are working together here. We need to address more than one to see meaningful improvement.
explainabilityMetadata.scientificFraming: Multiple converging mechanisms exceed activation threshold without a single dominant posterior; treatment combinatorics required.

legacyDiagnosisKeysNotMappedToCauses.rationale: Not a cause; surfaced via eligibility + objective routing.
Pigmentation phenotype, not a hair-loss cause.
Behavioral; routed to a non-cause behavioral pathway.
